# Mātuposakajātaka (Ja 455)

**ID:** Ja 455
**Section:** Jātaka (ja)
**Collection:** Suttas-Late-1
**Title (Pali):** Mātuposakajātaka
**Title (English, SuttaCentral):** The Elephant Who Cared for His Mother
**SuttaCentral:** https://suttacentral.net/ja455
**tipitaka.org (CST):** https://tipitaka.org/romn/cscd/s0513m.mul10.xml

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature and SuttaCentral)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and SuttaCentral data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Mātuposakajātaka* (Ja 455), also known as the *Mātiposaka-jātaka* or *Matuposaka Nāgarāja Jātaka*, is located in the eleventh nipāta (*Ekādasakanipāta*) of the Jātaka collection [Burlingame 1921b; Morris 1882; SuttaCentral]. In its frame narrative set at Jetavana, the Buddha recounts the story in response to a monk who was supporting his mother, observing that wise beings of old exercised filial devotion even when reborn in the animal realm [SuttaCentral].

In the story of the past, the Bodhisatta is an elephant living in the forest who faithfully provides for his blind mother [Appleton 2010; SuttaCentral]. After he rescues a lost traveler and guides him out of the wilderness, the man returns to civilization and betrays the Bodhisatta to the king's elephant-catchers [Appleton 2010]. Taken into royal captivity—where he is identified in the *Dhammapada-aṭṭhakathā* as the elephant Dhanapāla—the Bodhisatta refuses all food for seven days, weeping for his helpless mother and proclaiming that he cannot eat without her [Appleton 2010; Burlingame 1921a; Burlingame 1921b; SuttaCentral]. Moved by his extraordinary filial piety, the king grants him freedom to return to his mother in the forest [Appleton 2010]. In Theravāda tradition, this narrative is praised as an exemplar of forbearance and meritorious duty, serving as the subject of sermon illustrations and festival gateway (*toraṇa*) art [Appleton 2010; Conze 1956].

SuttaCentral registers four modern translations in four languages [SuttaCentral]. Machine text analysis by DharmaNexus identifies 18 Pali-internal text-reuse alignments across two commentaries: 14 matches with the *Jātaka-aṭṭhakathā* (Catuttho bhāgo, including the segment sequence §4.4–7.4 aligned with §834_2–847) and 4 matches with the *Cariyāpiṭaka-aṭṭhakathā* (§4.1–6.4 aligned with §895–901) [DharmaNexus]. No cross-language matches scoring 10 or above are identified [DharmaNexus].

**Parallels and text reuse**

- Text reuse within the Pali corpus (DharmaNexus): Jātaka-aṭṭhakathā (Catuttho bhāgo) (Atk S0513a4) (§4.4–7.4 ↔ §834_2–847); Cariyāpiṭaka-aṭṭhakathā (Atk S0512a) (§4.1–6.4 ↔ §895–901)

**Sources**

- [SuttaCentral] SuttaCentral record for ja455 — Provided titles, nidāna summary, narrative plot elements, and translation count.
- [DharmaNexus] DharmaNexus database — Provided text-reuse alignments with the Jātaka-aṭṭhakathā and Cariyāpiṭaka-aṭṭhakathā.
- [Appleton 2010] Naomi Appleton, Jātaka Stories in Theravāda Buddhism: Narrating the Bodhisatta Path (2010) — Supplied the detailed narrative of the betrayal, release, and modern artistic use on toraṇas.
- [Burlingame 1921a] Eugene Watson Burlingame, Buddhist Legends: Translated from the Original Pali Text of the Dhammapada Commentary, Part 1 (1921) — Reported the alternative title Matuposaka Nāgarāja Jātaka and the elephant name Dhanapāla.
- [Burlingame 1921b] Eugene Watson Burlingame, Buddhist Legends: Translated from the Original Pali Text of the Dhammapada Commentary, Part 3 (1921) — Confirmed the placement in the Eleventh Book and relation to Dhammapada verse 324.
- [Conze 1956] Edward Conze, Buddhist Meditation (1956) — Noted the story's use as an exemplar of the Bodhisatta's virtue of forbearance.
- [Morris 1882] Richard Morris, The Cariyā-Piṭaka (1882) — Noted the placement of the Jātaka in the Ekādasakanipāta.
